name: Fourth Lateran Council
informalName: The general council of the Lateran
teaser: Rome, 1215. Pope Innocent III held a general council at the Lateran. Its canons set out the faith, with the bread and wine changed in substance, bound every believer to confess at least once a year, ordered action against heretics and rebuked the Greeks.
knownFor: The council of Innocent III that named the change of bread and wine in substance, bound every believer to yearly confession and Easter communion, and condemned Joachim of Fiore's tract on the Trinity.
datesNote: 1215, the year the Annals of the Four Masters and Nicolaus Glassberger give. Hethum of Korykos enters it under the Armenian year 664, which his editors convert as 27 January 1215 to 26 January 1216, and a papal catalogue printed by Franz Ehrle puts it in Innocent's eighteenth year. The Annals of Ulster and of Kilronan, as John O'Donovan quotes them, enter it under 1216. No source we draw on from the time gives a month or day. By Carl Mirbt's dating it met from 11 to 30 November 1215; Ghewond Alishan gives 11 November
issue: Hethum of Korykos, an Armenian chronicler whose table its editors date to 1296, says Pope Innocent held a general council to tear Jerusalem from the hands of the unbelievers.

The notice of the council in Mansi's collection, an early-modern editor's summary reprinted in the Patrologia Latina, gives three aims: to correct the corrupt morals of the people, to condemn heretics, and to turn princes and people to the recovery of the Holy Land.

Abbot Joachim of Fiore had written a tract against Peter Lombard on the unity of the Trinity. In it he called Lombard a heretic and a madman for saying in his Sentences that there is one supreme reality which is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. By the canon's report, Joachim held that this made the shared essence a fourth beside the three persons, and he took the unity of the three to be like that of many people called one people (canon 2). The tract itself is not among our sources.

Canon 4 gives the Latin charge against the Greeks: since their church had withdrawn from obedience to Rome, Greeks had washed altars where Latin priests had celebrated, as though defiled, and had baptized again those the Latins had baptized; some, it says, still did.

Canon 3 condemns every heresy raised against the catholic faith, by whatever names its followers go. It names no group. The names Albigenses and Waldenses come from Heinrich Denzinger's headings of 1911.
calledBy: Innocent III. The notice in Mansi says he called it and presided over it. A variant manuscript of Pulkava's Bohemian chronicle, printed in its editor's note, says letters went out from the pope through the world in 1213 about calling a council, beginning "Vineam Domini Sabaoth". That letter is not among our sources
attended: No list of names and no account from inside the sessions is among our sources.

Hethum of Korykos counts 422 bishops and 72 archbishops. The Maronite patriarch and historian Istifan al-Duwayhi gives 411 bishops from the East and the West; his Arabic text is badly read in our copy and is used only as a second witness. The papal catalogue printed by Ehrle says almost the body of the whole universal church came together. The count in the notice in Mansi is unreadable in our copy.

The Maronite patriarch was there. Jacques de Vitry writes that the Maronites kept the customs and rites of the Latins as a sign of obedience, and so their patriarch came to the general council of the Lateran under Innocent III. Vitry does not name him; al-Duwayhi calls him Jeremiah (second witness only).
Fulk, bishop of Toulouse, went with Dominic, by the account of Jordan of Saxony, Dominic's successor as master of the Preachers.

Irish bishops came. The Annals of the Four Masters, in O'Donovan's English, say Dionysius O'Lonargan, archbishop of Cashel, died at Rome, and Conar O'Heney, bishop of Killaloe, died on his way home from the council. The Annals of Ulster, quoted in O'Donovan's notes, say Eghdon Mac Gilluir, coarb of Patrick and primate of Ireland, died at Rome after the general council.
Whether Francis of Assisi was there: the Observant Franciscan chronicler Nicolaus Glassberger says Francis met Dominic at the council. No earlier source among ours puts Francis there.
decided: Canon 1 set out the faith: one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit; one universal church of the faithful, outside which no one at all is saved; Christ's body and blood truly contained in the sacrament of the altar under the forms of bread and wine, the bread changed in substance into the body and the wine into the blood by God's power. Only a rightly ordained priest can make this sacrament. Baptism profits children and adults alike, a fallen Christian can be restored by penance, and married people too can reach eternal blessedness.

Canon 2 condemned Joachim's tract. With the approval of the council, the pope believed and confessed with Peter Lombard. Whoever defends Joachim's teaching on this point is to be refuted as a heretic. The monastery of Fiore was spared, because its rule was sound and, above all, because Joachim had ordered all his writings handed to Rome to be approved or corrected, in a letter he signed with his own hand. The same canon condemned the teaching of Almaric as not so much heretical as mad, without saying what it was.

Canon 3 dealt with heretics. The condemned were left to the secular powers for punishment; suspects who did not clear themselves were excommunicated, and after a year condemned as heretics. Rulers were to swear publicly to drive out from their lands all heretics marked out by the church; a lord who would not was excommunicated, and after a year the pope might free his vassals and offer his land to Catholics. Those who took the cross against heretics gained the Holy Land indulgence. Those who preached without authority from the apostolic see or the bishop of the place were excommunicated. Bishops were to visit their parishes once or twice a year and put men on oath to name heretics; a negligent bishop was to be deposed.

Canon 4 said the pope wished to cherish and honor the Greeks returning to obedience, bearing with their customs and rites as far as he could in the Lord. It forbade the washing of altars and the second baptism, "that there may be one fold and one shepherd", on pain of excommunication and deposition.
Canon 5 ranked the patriarchs after Rome: Constantinople first, Alexandria second, Antioch third, Jerusalem fourth.

Canon 21 bound every believer of either sex, past the age of discretion, to confess all their sins at least once a year to their own priest, to do the penance given, and to receive communion at least at Easter, unless their priest advised a pause for a reasonable cause. Whoever refused was to be barred from the church in life and denied Christian burial. A priest who revealed a confession was to be deposed and shut in a strict monastery for life.

Canons 23 to 26 ruled on the election of bishops, canon 62 forbade the sale of relics and the public veneration of newly found ones without the pope's approval, and the crusade decree made the clergy give a twentieth of their church income for three years to the Holy Land, with some religious and the crusaders themselves excepted; the pope and cardinals would pay a full tenth.
Canon 13, as the Bollandists quote it from Labbe, forbade anyone to found a new religious order: whoever wished to enter religion was to take one already approved.
outcome: When Dominic and Fulk asked for the order, Innocent told Dominic to go back to his brothers, choose with them a rule already approved and return for confirmation. With the council over, they went back and chose the rule of Augustine (Jordan of Saxony). Honorius III confirmed the order (the second Life of Dominic). The Bollandists, in the eighteenth century, connect Innocent's answer with canon 13.

Innocent died at Perugia in July 1216. Jacques de Vitry found the body there, stripped of its robes in the night and left almost naked in the church. The cardinals elected Honorius the next day (Vitry's letter of October 1216).

On 2 December 1216 Honorius III ordered the bishop of Lucca to stop defaming the abbot and monks of Fiore as heretics on the ground that Innocent, with the council's approval, had condemned Joachim's tract. A letter of Honorius dated 27 December 1220, as the Bollandists print it, orders it proclaimed through all Calabria that he holds Joachim to have been a Catholic man; Henry Charles Lea also dates to 1220 a bull calling Joachim a good Catholic.

The censure of Joachim passed into Gregory IX's Decretals, as Heinrich Denifle notes, and in 1255 the commission at Anagni judged that a passage of Joachim's Concordia seemed still to assert the heresy condemned in the Lateran council.

The Franciscan Salimbene wrote that the pope had ordained that there should be no new order of religious mendicants, but that this was not kept, through the negligence of the prelates. At Lyon in 1274 the Lateran canon was renewed, and the Carmelites and Augustinians were allowed to exist on sufferance, by Lea's account.
At Trent, the eighth canon on penance anathematizes anyone who says the faithful are not bound to confess once a year according to the constitution of the great Lateran council (Mirbt).

By the end of March 1217 Jacques de Vitry could write that the patriarch of the Maronites, with his archbishops, bishops and people, had left all errors and submitted to the Catholic faith and the obedience of the Roman church.

Nearly six centuries later the Pedalion, the Orthodox canon-law book of Agapios and Nikodemos of Mount Athos (first printed in 1800), called the council a local synod held in the Lateran of Rome in 1215. It cited canon 4 as proof, by the testimony of the Greeks' own enemies, that the Easterners then baptized Westerners who came over.

record.note: Mirbt gives the days 11 to 30 November; Lea and Denifle trace canon 2 and canon 13 into later law and councils.

traditions.name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
traditions.note: Innocent III called the council and presided (the notice in Mansi); canon 5 calls the Roman church mother and teacher of all Christ's faithful.

traditions.name: Maronite Christianity
traditions.note: Its patriarch came to the council, Jacques de Vitry writes, and by 1217 had submitted with his bishops and people to the Roman church.

traditions.name: The Dominican Order
traditions.note: Dominic came with Fulk of Toulouse to ask Innocent to confirm an order of Preachers, and after the council the brothers took Augustine's rule (Jordan of Saxony).

traditions.name: Joachimite Current
traditions.note: Canon 2 condemned Joachim's tract against Peter Lombard and spared his monastery; Honorius III later forbade the monks to be called heretics.

traditions.name: Cathars / Albigensians
traditions.note: Canon 3 condemned all heretics, and canon 1 affirmed that married people too can be saved; the canons name no group, and the name Albigenses is Denzinger's heading.

traditions.name: The Waldensians
traditions.note: Canon 3 excommunicated those who preached without authority from the pope or bishop; the canon names no group, and the name Waldenses is Denzinger's heading.

traditions.name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
traditions.note: Canon 4 rebuked the Greeks for washing altars and baptizing again; the Pedalion later called the council a local synod and cited the canon.

traditions.name: The Franciscan Movement
traditions.note: Salimbene, a Franciscan, complained that the council's ban on new orders of mendicants was not kept.

traditions.name: The Carmelites
traditions.note: When the Lateran canon on new orders was renewed at Lyon in 1274, the Carmelites were allowed to exist on sufferance (Lea).

uncertain: No account from inside the sessions is among our sources, and the canons are held only in extracts printed by Mirbt and Denzinger and in the Bollandists' quotation of canon 13. Canons 67 to 70, on the Jews, are not among them; the full acts, in Mansi tome 22, are not held.

The count: Hethum gives 422 bishops and 72 archbishops; al-Duwayhi, a second witness only, gives 411 bishops; the count in the notice in Mansi is unreadable in our copy. No source among ours gives a number of abbots.

The days, 11 to 30 November, are Mirbt's dating, and the opening on 11 November is also Alishan's; Alishan wrongly calls it a council held at Lyon. No source we draw on from the time gives a month or day. The Annals of Ulster and of Kilronan enter the council under 1216.

Whether the council was general or local: Denzinger and the notice in Mansi number it the twelfth ecumenical council, and Vitry and the Irish annals call it general; the Pedalion calls it a local synod, and John Covel, an Anglican writer of 1722, calls it a pretended general council.
Whether Francis was there rests on Glassberger alone.
What canon 13 forbade: the Bollandists' quotation forbids any new religious order; Salimbene reads it as a ban on new orders of mendicants.

Innocent's death day: the notice in Mansi, after the Ursberg chronicler, and Glassberger give the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August (17 July); the catalogue printed by Ehrle gives the tenth (23 July).

The 1220 letter on Joachim: our copy prints two columns interleaved, so the passage on Calabria and the date of 27 December 1220 are read as part of Honorius's letter to the archbishop of Cosenza and the bishop of Bisignano; Lea agrees on a bull of 1220.
The Maronite patriarch's name, and the pallium al-Duwayhi says the pope gave him, rest on al-Duwayhi alone, read as a second witness.
